turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have been acquainted with his sufferings, and I cannot wonder that they have rendered him in some degree careless of the general propriety of his conduct. But I am far from despising him on that account. I rather esteem him for his attachment to those who have always retained their affection for him, in spite of his ungracious behavior.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that your opinion of Mr. Wickham is based on a partial, erroneous account. His true character is far less amiable than you suppose.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am not surprised at your interference on behalf of your friend, Mr. Darcy. But why did you feel the need to deceive me about his character?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must beg you, Miss Bennet, to consider the reasons behind my actions. My pride and my sense of duty have often led me to act against my better nature. I have erred, but I hope to make amends.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your pride, Mr. Darcy, has indeed been your greatest misfortune. It has made you blind to the wrongs you have committed, and it has led you to treat others with a coldness and disdain that are unforgivable. But if you are truly determined to make amends, I hope you will prove yourself worthy of forgiveness.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I acknowledge the justice of your words, Miss Bennet. My pride has indeed been my downfall, and I am resolved to amend my ways. If I may, I wish to express my deepest feelings towards you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I must confess that I am both astonished and perplexed by your declaration. My feelings towards you have long been defined by your actions, and they have not been favorable.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I understand the difficulty of your position, Miss Bennet, but I cannot help the feelings I have for you. They are sincere and profound, despite my evident failings in your estimation.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your affection comes as a surprise, and I must admit, it is not one I am prepared to return. Your actions have left me with little reason to trust your sentiments.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I am acutely aware of the disparity between my actions and the sentiments I now express. I have wronged you and others, but I pledge to earn your trust and respect through my conduct.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your words reveal a change, Mr. Darcy, but they also remind me of your past failings. It will take more than promises to alter the opinion I have formed of you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I do not expect to alter your opinion quickly or easily. I am aware of the burden I must bear, but I am also resolved to prove myself worthy of your regard.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your resolve is commendable, but I cannot overlook the past. I will observe your actions and judge accordingly.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I understand the gravity of your words and shall strive to live up to them.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I appreciate your sincerity, but I must reserve my judgment until I see tangible changes in your conduct.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I will do everything in my power to earn back your esteem and prove my sincerity.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I trust your words, Mr. Darcy, but actions will speak louder than words.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I will ensure that my actions do indeed speak louder than words.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I am well aware of your wealth and your station, but I cannot disregard my own feelings and the opinions I hold of you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I understand your reservations. My actions have indeed been the source of much misunderstanding and discord. I will strive to change them.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
